briefs.solution: A supersession-based edit path: editing a signed document creates a new version, the signed original is frozen and retained, and a fresh approval circuit runs on the new version — with a visible audit trail linking the two.

challenges.headline: Unscoped 'any manager, any document'
challenges.premise: The request names only 'managers' as the actor, with no restriction on which documents can be edited after signature.
challenges.alternative: Restricting eligibility by classification (e.g. internal policies yes, signed client contracts no) keeps the feature from accidentally reopening documents where post-signature edits are legally or contractually inappropriate.
challenges.consequence: Without scoping, any manager could reopen any signed document — including ones where that action has legal consequences the platform has no way to prevent.
challenges.recommendation: Define eligible document types/classifications with the client before building the trigger.

challenges.headline: Re-approval circuit assumed identical
challenges.premise: The workflow assumes a 'fresh approval circuit' runs, implicitly mirroring the original signatories one-for-one.
challenges.alternative: Since an edit may materially change the document's content, the re-approval circuit could reasonably differ from the original — e.g. add a compliance reviewer for substantive changes — rather than always replaying the same signatories.
challenges.consequence: Assuming the same circuit reduces friction but risks under-scrutinizing edits that a client would actually want a different or additional reviewer to see.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with the client whether re-approval circuit composition should be configurable or always mirror the original.

challenges.headline: Approval vs. 'current' conflated mid-edit
challenges.premise: The request treats 'edit and re-approve' as a single action, without addressing what readers see while the new version is awaiting approval.
challenges.alternative: Because approval and publication are separate lifecycles in this system, the old signed version can stay 'current' and visible until the new version clears approval — avoiding a gap where no valid current version exists.
challenges.consequence: If this isn't decided, the build may either hide the document during review (disrupting users who need it) or expose an unapproved draft as if it were authoritative.
challenges.recommendation: Explicitly define what is shown as 'current' during the re-approval window before implementing the edit path.

challenges.headline: 'Edit and re-approve' implies in-place change
challenges.premise: The request frames this as editing a signed document and re-approving it, as if it were a normal content update.
challenges.alternative: Treat any change to a signed document as supersession: freeze the original, create a new version, and re-open approval on that new version — mirroring how the platform already treats contract amendments.
challenges.consequence: Building a simple in-place edit would break the frozen-after-approval guarantee, invalidate prior signatures silently, and leave the audit trail unable to show what changed.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm explicitly with the client that this is a supersession workflow, not a content patch, before estimating.

challenges.headline: Manager as sole re-approver
challenges.premise: The request names managers as the ones who edit and re-approve, suggesting they alone validate the new version.
challenges.alternative: Route re-approval back through the original signatory circuit (or an explicitly defined subset), since the new version's legal standing depends on who actually signs it.
challenges.consequence: If a manager can unilaterally re-approve content that was originally signed by others, the new signature may not carry the same legal or organizational weight — undermining e-signature validity.
challenges.recommendation: Clarify with legal/compliance whether the original signatories must re-approve, or whether a defined delegate circuit is acceptable.

challenges.headline: Approved conflated with published
challenges.premise: The request implicitly assumes that re-approving the edited document makes it the version people see and act on.
challenges.alternative: Keep publication a separate, explicit step: an edited-and-re-approved version can exist without automatically superseding what's currently published, until someone deliberately republishes it.
challenges.consequence: Without this separation, a re-approval could silently change what readers see mid-workflow, or conversely, an approved correction could fail to reach readers who need it — both are classic sources of people acting on the wrong version.
challenges.recommendation: Define, with the client, whether re-approval auto-supersedes the published version or requires a separate publish action.

challenges.headline: 'Edit' assumed to mean in-place change
challenges.premise: The request says managers should 'edit and re-approve' a signed document, which reads as a direct modification of existing content.
challenges.alternative: Model the edit as creating a new version while the old signed version is retained and marked superseded — this preserves prior signatures, citations and audit integrity instead of overwriting them.
challenges.consequence: If built as a true in-place edit, it silently invalidates the original signature and any prior reference to that content, which is a serious problem for a system whose value proposition is legal traceability.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with the client that 'edit' means 'supersede with a new version,' and design the data model around versioning before any UI work starts.

challenges.headline: Re-approval circuit composition unclear

challenges.alternative: Reuse the original multi-step approval circuit for re-approval, or explicitly define a lighter validation path — but make the choice deliberately rather than defaulting to manager self-approval.
challenges.consequence: Letting the editor also be the sole approver undermines segregation of duties and weakens the audit trail's credibility exactly where compliance scrutiny will focus.
challenges.recommendation: Clarify with the client (and likely compliance/legal) whether the original signatories must re-approve or a distinct lighter circuit is acceptable.

challenges.headline: Publication state during re-approval

challenges.alternative: Keep the previously published version live and marked 'current' until the new version completes re-approval and is explicitly published, rather than pulling or replacing it the moment editing starts.
challenges.consequence: Without this rule, readers can either lose access to a valid document mid-review or end up acting on a stale version once the new one is silently in place — the exact 'approved ≠ published' confusion this domain is prone to.
challenges.recommendation: Define the publication transition rule (when the old version is stamped superseded, and when the new one goes live) before implementation.

next_steps: Confirm with the client that editing a signed document means creating a new superseding version, not modifying signed content in place.
Define who can trigger this edit (role and/or classification scope) and whether re-approval must involve the original signatories or a lighter circuit.
Specify what happens to the previously published version during the re-approval window — held as current, or immediately marked pending.
Confirm the audit trail and export requirements expected for compliance before implementation starts.

decisions.decision: The underlying object model follows the standard Document / Version / Approval / Signatory pattern.
An audit trail covering edits and re-approvals will be built in from the start rather than added later.
decisions.why: Signed documents are compliance-sensitive, and retrofitting audit history after the fact is expensive and risky.
decisions.alternative: Treat audit logging as a secondary feature added once the core edit/re-approval flow works.
decisions.tradeoff: More upfront engineering effort in exchange for avoiding a costly, high-risk retrofit later.
